subject: HSS
title: Continuity and Change (Local History)
description: Third-grade history–social science focused on the student's own region: its physical geography, the American Indian nations who have lived there since long ago and today, the explorers, missions, ranchos and settlers who changed it, and how the local community was founded and has changed over time. Students also learn about rules, laws, citizenship and the three branches of government, national symbols and heroes, and the local economy, using maps, photographs, oral histories and other primary sources.
framework: California History–Social Science Content Standards; 2016 CA History–Social Science Framework

standards.3.1: Students describe the physical and human geography and use maps, tables, graphs, photographs and charts to organize information about people, places and environments in a spatial context.
standards.3.1.1: Identify geographical features in their local region (deserts, mountains, valleys, hills, coastal areas, oceans, lakes).
standards.3.1.2: Trace the ways in which people have used the resources of the local region and modified the physical environment (dams, cultivation, buildings).
standards.3.2: Students describe the American Indian nations in their local region long ago and in the recent past.
standards.3.2.1: Describe national identities, religious beliefs, customs and various folklore traditions of local American Indian nations.
standards.3.2.2: Discuss the ways in which physical geography, including climate, influenced how local Indian nations adapted to their natural environment (food, clothing, tools).
standards.3.2.3: Describe the economy and systems of government, particularly those with tribal constitutions, and their relationship to federal and state governments.
standards.3.2.4: Discuss the interaction of new settlers with the already established Indians of the region.
standards.3.3: Students draw from historical and community resources to organize the sequence of local historical events and describe how each period of settlement left its mark on the land.
standards.3.3.1: Research the explorers who visited here, the newcomers who settled here, and the people who continue to come to the region, including their cultural and religious traditions and contributions.
standards.3.3.2: Describe the economies established by settlers and their influence on the present-day economy, with emphasis on private property and entrepreneurship.
standards.3.3.3: Trace why their community was established, how individuals and families contributed to its founding and development, and how it has changed over time, drawing on maps, photographs, oral histories, letters, newspapers and other primary sources.
standards.3.4: Students understand the role of rules and laws in our daily lives and the basic structure of the U.S. government.
standards.3.4.1: Determine the reasons for rules, laws and the U.S. Constitution; the role of citizenship in promoting rules and laws; and the consequences for people who violate rules and laws.
standards.3.4.2: Discuss the importance of public virtue and the role of citizens, including how to participate in a classroom, in the community and in civic life.
standards.3.4.3: Know the histories of important local and national landmarks, symbols and essential documents that create a sense of community among citizens and exemplify cherished ideals (flag, bald eagle, Statue of Liberty, Constitution, Declaration of Independence, U.S. Capitol).
standards.3.4.4: Understand the three branches of government, with an emphasis on local government.
standards.3.4.5: Describe the ways in which California, the other states and sovereign American Indian tribes contribute to the making of our nation and participate in the federal system of government.
standards.3.4.6: Describe the lives of American heroes who took risks to secure our freedoms (e.g., Anne Hutchinson, Benjamin Franklin, Thomas Jefferson, Abraham Lincoln, Frederick Douglass, Harriet Tubman, Martin Luther King Jr.).
standards.3.5: Students demonstrate basic economic reasoning skills and an understanding of the economy of the local region.
standards.3.5.1: Describe the ways in which local producers have used and are using natural, human and capital resources to produce goods and services in the past and the present.
standards.3.5.2: Understand that some goods are made locally, some elsewhere in the United States and some abroad.
standards.3.5.3: Understand that individual economic choices involve trade-offs and the evaluation of benefits and costs.
standards.3.5.4: Discuss the relationship of students' 'work' in school and their personal human capital.

units.title: Our Land: Geography of Our Region
units.big_idea: Landforms, water and climate shape where and how people live in our region.

units.title: The First Peoples of Our Region
units.big_idea: American Indian nations adapted to the land, built rich cultures and continue as sovereign nations today.

units.title: Newcomers: Explorers, Missions and Ranchos
units.big_idea: Explorers and settlers brought great change to the region and to its first peoples.

units.title: Building Our Community Over Time
units.big_idea: Every community has a story of founders, newcomers and change that we can uncover with primary sources.

units.title: Rules, Laws and Good Citizens
units.big_idea: Rules and laws protect people, and good citizens help their communities.

units.title: How Government Works
units.big_idea: Our government has three branches at local, state and national levels, and tribes are sovereign nations within the federal system.

units.title: American Symbols, Landmarks and Heroes
units.big_idea: Symbols, documents and heroes remind us of shared ideals like freedom and equality.

units.title: Our Local Economy
units.big_idea: People use resources to produce goods and services, and every economic choice has a trade-off.

units.title: Community History Showcase
units.big_idea: Historians share what they learn so others can understand their community.
